newsitem.title: DUBAI: More than 200 dead in big Iran earthquake.
newsitem.headline: More than 200 dead in big Iran earthquake.

text.p: More than 200 people were killed and hundreds injured on Saturday when a powerful earthquake measuring 7.1 on the Richter scale rocked rural areas of eastern Iran, the official Iranian news agency IRNA said.

Mehdi Siadati, head of the disaster relief agency in Darmian district of Khorasan province, said the quake levelled 11 villages and inflicted heavy damage on the towns of Qaen and Birjand near its epicentre about 150 km (90 miles) from the border with Afghanistan.
Siadati said teams had been rushed to stricken areas and a headquarters had been set up to manage relief operations.
Mojtaba Sadeqian, governor of Qaen district, said the quake wreaked havoc in rural areas at the foot of Qaen mountain.
Iranian television said the village of Zirkuh in Qaen district had been severely hit by the earthquake, which struck at 12:28 p.m. (0758 GMT).

Mashhad, Iran's second largest city with a population of about two million, was jolted by the quake. It was felt up to 800 km (500 miles) away in nearby provinces and another city where it caused panic, IRNA said.
A shopkeeper in Qaen, a town of about 25,000 people, told Reuters by telephone there was no apparent widespread damage there but he had heard several outlying villages were badly hit.

The stricken area is significantly less densely populated than a region near the Caspian Sea coast where 35,000 people were killed by an earthquake measuring 7.3 in 1990. That quake was the worst registered in Iran, which is frequently hit by earthquakes.
At least 1,000 people were killed and more than 36,000 made homeless when a quake measuring 5.5 on the Richter scale hit northwest Iran in February.
The Geophysics Institute in Mashhad put the latest quake's epicentre 370 km (230 miles) southeast of the city.
IRNA said the quake caused panic as far away as the city of Kashan, south of the capital Tehran, where people said they saw water in ponds spill over.
A journalist in Mashhad, capital of Iran's northeastern Khorasan province bordering Afghanistan and Turkmenistan, said there was no apparent widespread damage in the city.

"I came to work on a bus and along my route everything seemed alright," the journalist told Reuters. "I did not see any signs of damage. But the quake was very strong and I am sure there is a lot of damage at its epicentre south of here."
Tehran radio said the quake, felt in three adjoining provinces, was centred near the towns of Qaen and Birjand

The U.S. Geological Survey based in Golden, Colorado measured the quake at 7.3 on the Richter scale at its epicentre. U.S. geophysicist Waverly Person said its focus was fairly shallow -- about 20 miles (30 km) below the earth's surface.
